theme: Letters to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira
readingInstruction: Read Revelation 2:1-29. Jesus speaks to four of the seven churches: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira. Notice the pattern in each letter: a description of Christ, what he knows, what he commends or criticizes, a call to listen, and a promise to the one who conquers.
settingTheScene: The seven churches were real congregations in cities of Asia Minor, arranged along a circular road. Each letter reflects its city’s setting: Ephesus, a great port and the center of the cult of Artemis; Smyrna, loyal to Rome, with a hostile Jewish community; Pergamum, with temples to Zeus, Asclepius, and the emperor; Thyatira, a city of trade guilds that required participation in pagan feasts. The letters also work as a mirror for churches of every age, because the problems of love grown cold, persecution, compromise, and tolerance of false teaching never go away.
observation: “But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first” (v. 4).
“Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first” (v. 5).
“To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God” (v. 7).
“Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (v. 10).
“Therefore repent. If not, I will come to you soon and war against them with the sword of my mouth” (v. 16).
“A white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it” (v. 17).
“I am he who searches mind and heart” (v. 23).
“And I will give him the morning star” (v. 28).
interpretation:
To Ephesus, Jesus is the one who walks among the lampstands. He commends their works, toil, patient endurance, and refusal to tolerate evil, and their testing of false apostles. “But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first.” They had kept the doctrine but lost the love. The remedy has three parts: “Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first.” If not, he will remove their lampstand. Correct doctrine without warm love is a dying church. The promise to the conqueror: “I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God,” the restoration of Eden.

To Smyrna, Jesus is “the first and the last, who died and came to life.” There is no criticism, only comfort. “I know your tribulation and your poverty (but you are rich).” They are slandered and about to suffer imprisonment. “Do not fear what you are about to suffer… Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.” Polycarp, the bishop of Smyrna, was martyred about sixty years later, saying he had served Christ eighty-six years. The promise: the conqueror “will not be hurt by the second death.” The first death can touch the body; the second cannot touch the faithful.

To Pergamum, Jesus has “the sharp two-edged sword.” The church lives “where Satan’s throne is,” probably a reference to the center of emperor worship. They have held fast his name, even when Antipas, “my faithful witness,” was killed. But some hold the teaching of Balaam (who led Israel into idolatry and sexual immorality, Numbers 25) and the Nicolaitans. The command: “Therefore repent.” The conqueror will receive “hidden manna” and a white stone with a new name, signs of provision and of acceptance and a personal identity from Christ.

To Thyatira, Jesus is the Son of God, “whose eyes are like a flame of fire.” This is the only place in Revelation he is called Son of God. The church is growing in love, faith, service, and patience, but “you tolerate that woman Jezebel,” who calls herself a prophetess and leads his servants into sexual immorality and food offered to idols. Jesus gave her time to repent, but she refuses. He warns: “I am he who searches mind and heart, and I will give to each of you as your works deserve.” Those who have not followed her teaching are to hold fast until he comes. The conqueror receives authority over the nations, sharing Christ’s rule (Psalm 2:8-9), and “the morning star,” which is Christ himself (22:16).

Each letter ends: “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.” The promises to the conqueror are not for a special class of believers. In 1 John 5:4-5, everyone born of God conquers through faith in Jesus. The conqueror is the persevering believer. Christ knows what we face, and he will keep his promises.
connection: Acts 19 tells of the founding of the church in Ephesus. Ephesians 6:23-24 speaks of love for the Lord. Genesis 2:9 and 3:22-24 describe the tree of life. Revelation 20:6 and 21:8 speak of the second death. Numbers 22-25 and 31:16 are the story of Balaam. 1 Kings 16:31-33 and 2 Kings 9 tell of Jezebel. Psalm 2:7-9 is the background of authority over the nations. 1 Corinthians 8 and 10:14-22 discuss food offered to idols. Jeremiah 17:10 and Romans 8:27 speak of God searching hearts. 2 Peter 1:19 and Revelation 22:16 mention the morning star. 1 John 5:4-5 says every believer conquers.
application:
Ask if your love for Christ and for his people is what it was at first. If not, follow the three steps: remember, repent, and return.

If you face pressure or ridicule for your faith, take the words to Smyrna to heart: do not fear; be faithful.

What teaching or practice do you tolerate that Christ would not? Bring it to him.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus that he walks among his churches and knows your works.
Ask him to give you endurance and faithfulness.
